coaching.overall_assessment: The 13.97-second sequence captured intermittent upward vertical hip propulsion, highlighted by velocity peaks at 4.9s (+0.23) and 6.3s (+0.26). The climber predominantly kept extended arm positions interspersed with brief, targeted deep flexion phases (notably on the left arm around 6.7s-6.9s and 13.1s-13.4s, and brief right arm engagements around 12.3s-12.5s). Lower limb metrics indicate dynamic foot adjustments and high-step loading, particularly through the right leg.
strengths: Efficient skeletal hanging: Between 2.1s and 6.3s, the left elbow consistently registered extended angles between 164° and 179°, which often indicates resting or moving with straight arms to reduce bicep and forearm fatigue.

Dynamic, non-prolonged lock-offs: Deep bend intervals were short (totaling 0.40s on the left arm and under 0.07s on the right arm), suggesting that arm flexion was applied dynamically to execute reach or movement rather than held in inefficient, sustained isometric lock-offs.
Vertical momentum generation: Pronounced upward vertical hip velocity peaks at 4.9s (0.230) and 6.3s (0.263) indicate effective explosive drive, likely initiating from lower body push.
improvements: Deadpoint timing and hip deceleration: Hip vertical velocity repeatedly dipped into negative values following dynamic upward efforts (e.g., -0.052 at 5.6s, -0.081 at 7.7s, and continuous negative drift between 9.8s and 11.9s). Work on catching target holds at the apex of the hip drive to prevent dropping momentum.

Weight transfer onto high feet: Between 8.4s and 12.6s, the right knee reached acute flexion angles (25.3° at 8.4s and 4.7° at 12.6s) while the left leg remained extended (~141°–165°). Focus on rolling the hips over high footholds and pressing smoothly through the toes to avoid abrupt deceleration and reduce strain during deep knee bends.
limitations: Significant occlusions and null data: Multiple key frames lacked joint angle tracking (e.g., left elbow angle was null across 0.0s–1.4s and 7.7s–11.2s; left knee was unrecorded for several seconds), preventing a complete picture of bilateral movement coordination.

Potential 2D tracking distortion: The extreme 4.66° angle recorded on the right knee at 12.6s likely reflects camera perspective foreshortening or landmark tracking error rather than true anatomical joint orientation.

Absence of route and wall context: The dataset lacks wall angle, hold types, and spatial positions, meaning observed body positions cannot be definitively judged as technically correct or sub-optimal relative to the specific beta.
